To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the postural fall in blood pressures is positively related to alcohol consumption and use of sleeping tablets, and negatively related with body mass index.
the magnitude of the postural fall in blood pressures is related to the intake of alcohol and sleeping pills, and to anxiety levels.
the magnitude of the postural fall in blood-pressure is not associated with age, sex, or hypertension treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of lifestyle factors in postural hypoten-sion in the elderly, a problem of increasing importance in an ageing population.
the relationship between lifestyle and the postural fall in blood presure in the elderly, and with the possible role of this fall in the development of cardiovascular diseases.

the development of a model for the assessment of postural fall in blood-pressure, and with the identification of lifestyle factors which are associated with postural fall in pressure in elderly people.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence for the role of alcohol in the genesis of hypertension is equivocal, and that the role of alcohol is probably not important in the genesis of essential hypertension.
the postural fall in blood-pressure in the elderly is not a function of the drugs used to treat hypertension, but is a consequence of other factors.
the evidence does not support the view that antihypertensive drug therapy increases the risk of falls.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the postural fall in blood-pressure was related to the use of sleeping-tablets and alcohol, and not to treatment for hypertension.
the use of sleeping pills and alcohol may increase the fall in systollic blood pressure on standing, and the use of sleeping pill and alcohol should be avoided.
the use of sleeping pills is associated with a greater fall in blood pressure when standing up, and that this may contribute to the increased risk of falls and hip fracture in the elderly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be careful about how we interpret the results of our studies, especially when we are looking at the relationship between a variable and its change over time.
postural fall is not related to drug treatment for hypertension.
we can’t just blame the drugs.
